# A Complete DataRaft Workflow in 15 Minutes {#sec-first-workflow}

This chapter uses the smallest verified path through the current API. It runs entirely in memory.

## Define expectations

```{.r}
library(dataraft)

policies <- dr_product("policies") |>
  dr_add_contract(c(
    policy_id = "integer",
    premium = "numeric"
  )) |>
  dr_add_quality(~ premium >= 0)
```

The product is a definition. No delivery has been accepted yet.

## Run a bad delivery

```{.r}
bad <- dr_run(
  policies,
  data = data.frame(
    policy_id = 1:2,
    premium = c(120, -20)
  ),
  write = FALSE,
  stop_on_failure = FALSE
)

bad$status
dataraft.core::dr_quality_rows(bad)
```

`write = FALSE` prevents a configured DataRaft writer from running. `stop_on_failure = FALSE` returns the blocked result so you can inspect it. The same pattern is used in the tested README examples in the current repository.

## Correct and collect

```{.r}
good <- dr_run(
  policies,
  data = data.frame(
    policy_id = 1:2,
    premium = c(120, 20)
  ),
  write = FALSE
)

dr_collect(good)
```

`dr_collect()` is intentionally defined on executed results, not product definitions. Trying to collect a product is an error because a definition is not data.

## The workflow on one page

```{.r}
library(dataraft)

policies <- dr_product("policies") |>
  dr_add_contract(c(policy_id = "integer", premium = "numeric")) |>
  dr_add_quality(~ premium >= 0)

result <- dr_run(
  policies,
  data = data.frame(policy_id = 1:3, premium = c(120, 80, 95)),
  write = FALSE
)

accepted <- dr_collect(result)
```

This small example already contains the essential method:

1. define the product;
2. state the expected shape;
3. state a business quality rule;
4. run one delivery;
5. accept data only from a successful result.

No storage choice is required yet.

::: {.callout-warning title="A successful R expression is not enough"}
The important status is the DataRaft run status and its checks, not whether the R process reached the end of the script.
:::

## Why not publish yet?

Publication adds a second concern: where accepted data should live. Keeping the first workflow in memory makes it easier to understand the logical gate before adding filesystem, database, or lake semantics.

In Chapter 9 we will attach an RDS target and then a governed lake target. The product definition can stay almost unchanged.

## Try it

Change `premium` to character data. Then add an extra column. Observe which failures come from the contract and which come from the quality rule. In the next chapter we will make those contract semantics explicit.

## Read the result as evidence, not just data

A successful run returns more than the rows. The result records a run identifier, status, validation status, timestamps, inputs, outputs, warnings, quality evidence, and the inspected product definition. This distinction matters because a recurring delivery has two questions: *what data did we get?* and *what happened while accepting it?* `dr_collect()` answers the first. The run result answers the second.

Keep those two questions separate in your own code. A useful pattern is to retain the result before collecting it:

```r
result <- dr_run(
  orders,
  data = incoming,
  write = FALSE,
  stop_on_failure = FALSE
)

result$status
result$validation_status
dr_quality_report(result)

if (result$status == "completed") {
  accepted <- dr_collect(result)
}
```

This is slightly more verbose than piping everything into `dr_collect()`, but it gives you a stable place to inspect warnings and failures. For an interactive analysis, the shorter pipe is often fine. For a repeated process, a named result object is easier to log, test, and hand to diagnostics.

### Why `write = FALSE` comes first

The first workflow deliberately runs without a configured writer. That lets you learn the validation path before persistence enters the picture. It also makes the boundary explicit: an accepted in-memory result is already useful. Publication is a separate decision.

`write = FALSE` does not promise that arbitrary user callbacks are free of side effects. It skips the configured DataRaft writer. Source readers or custom transformation functions are ordinary R code and can still perform their own I/O. This is one reason the book starts with plain data frames and declarative recipes.

::: {.callout-tip title="Try it"}
Change one thing at a time. Add an unexpected column, remove `amount`, make one amount negative, and then duplicate an `id` after adding a keyed contract. Save the result with `stop_on_failure = FALSE` and compare the quality reports. The goal is to learn the shape of failure evidence before you add storage.
:::

## Exercises

1. Run the same product definition against three deliveries: valid data, a negative premium, and a missing `premium` column. Compare the returned status and quality evidence.
2. Keep `stop_on_failure = FALSE` and write a small function that returns only accepted data while preserving the failed result for diagnostics.
3. Add a key to the contract and create a duplicate policy identifier. Explain why this failure is different from a negative premium.
